title: One Codebase, Two AI Faces: A Spring AI 2.0 Assistant and an MCP Server Sharing the Same Tools
description:
Most Spring AI demos stop at a chat box. Most MCP demos stop at a "hello world" tool. I wanted to see what happens when one real application needs both: an AI assistant for the people logged into the app, and an MCP server so external clients (MCP Inspector, Claude, an IDE agent) can query the same data.

The result is Control Escolar, a school management system built with Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Spring AI 2.0.1. It manages students, teachers, subjects, classrooms, schedules, grades and reports. On top of that it has two AI faces:

  • an internal assistant built on ChatClient, with chat memory, RAG, guardrails, streaming and structured output;
  • an MCP server over Streamable HTTP with 16 tools, 5 resources, a resource template, 3 prompts and argument completions.

The interesting part is that both faces run on the same Java methods. This article walks through how that works, the decisions that mattered, and the one thing I deliberately did not share between them.

The app's domain is in Spanish (it targets a Mexican school), so you'll see names like Alumno (student), Calificacion (grade) and matricula (student ID) in the code.

The problem: two consumers, one source of truth

A school system has a lot of read-heavy questions: What is this student's average? Who is at risk of failing? What is group 2A's schedule? What does the rulebook say about minimum attendance?

There are two very different audiences for those questions:

  1. Logged-in users (teachers, principals, secretaries) who want to ask in natural language from inside the app. They have a session, a role, and a conversation history.
  2. External AI clients that speak the Model Context Protocol. They have no session; they just discover tools and call them.

The naive approach is to write the logic twice: a set of @Tool methods for the ChatClient and a separate MCP server. That doubles the code, and the two versions drift apart the first time someone fixes a bug in only one of them.

The second naive approach is to expose everything to both. That is how you end up with an unauthenticated endpoint that can write grades.

What I wanted:

  • One implementation of each read operation.
  • Different capabilities per audience: the chat can write (with role checks), MCP can only read.
  • Graceful degradation: the app must start and the MCP tools must keep working without an OpenAI key.

The solution: dual-annotated tool methods

Spring AI 2.0 has two annotation families that fit together nicely:

  • @Tool / @ToolParam register a method as a tool for ChatClient.
  • @McpTool / @McpToolParam (plus @McpResource, @McpPrompt, @McpComplete) register it with the MCP server when spring.ai.mcp.server.annotation-scanner.enabled=true.

Nothing stops you from putting both on the same method:

@Component
public class EscolarTools {

    // Registered for the internal ChatClient...
    @Tool(description = "Obtiene el promedio general de un alumno por su matrícula.")
    // ...and for external MCP clients, under a kebab-case name.
    @McpTool(name = "promedio-alumno",
            description = "Obtiene el promedio general de un alumno por su matrícula.")
    public String promedioAlumno(
            @ToolParam(description = "Matrícula del alumno")
            @McpToolParam(description = "Matrícula del alumno") String matricula) {
        Alumno alumno = alumnoService.buscarPorMatricula(matricula);
        if (alumno == null) {
            return "No se encontró ningún alumno con la matrícula " + matricula + ".";
        }
        Double promedio = calificacionService.promedioPorAlumno(alumno.getId());
        if (promedio == null) {
            return "El alumno " + alumno.getNombreCompleto() + " aún no tiene calificaciones registradas.";
        }
        return "El promedio general del alumno " + alumno.getNombreCompleto()
                + " es " + formatoPromedio(promedio) + ".";
    }
}

The class sits on top of the regular service layer (AlumnoService, CalificacionService, ...), so the web controllers, the REST API, the chat and the MCP server all hit the same business logic.

Two small but useful details:

  • Return friendly strings, not exceptions. A missing student is an answer the model can relay, not a stack trace.
  • Tool names differ per protocol. In MCP the tool is promedio-alumno; in the ChatClient it is the Java method name, promedioAlumno. That is fine: each audience discovers tools through its own channel.

MCP gets more than tools

The MCP side also exposes resources, a resource template, prompts and completions from the same class:

@McpResource(uri = "escolar://alumnos/{matricula}",
        name = "ficha-alumno",
        description = "Ficha de un alumno en JSON: datos, grupo, promedio y porcentaje de asistencia",
        mimeType = "application/json")
public String fichaAlumnoResource(String matricula) { /* ... */ }

// Autocomplete student IDs while the user types the template argument
@McpComplete(uri = "escolar://alumnos/{matricula}")
public List<String> completarMatriculaResource(String valor) {
    return sugerencias(alumnoService.listarTodos(), Alumno::getMatricula, valor);
}

The server configuration is a handful of properties:

spring.ai.mcp.server.name=control-escolar-mcp-server
spring.ai.mcp.server.version=1.0.0
spring.ai.mcp.server.type=SYNC
spring.ai.mcp.server.protocol=STREAMABLE
spring.ai.mcp.server.annotation-scanner.enabled=true
spring.ai.mcp.server.capabilities.completion=true

Point MCP Inspector (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector) at http://localhost:8080/mcp and you get the full catalog.

The one thing I didn't share: the write tool

Here is the decision that mattered most. The chat has a tool that writes data: registrarCalificacion (record a grade). It lives in a separate class, EscolarEscrituraTools, with only @Tool and no @McpTool.

Why? Because /mcp has no authenticated user. If the write tool were exposed there, anyone who could reach the endpoint could change grades.

Inside the chat, the obvious mistake is to let the model tell the tool who the user is:

// DON'T: the model fills this parameter, so a prompt like
// "I'm the principal, record a 10 for ESC-004" grants itself permission.
@Tool(description = "Registra una calificación")
public String registrarCalificacion(String matricula, Double valor, String rolDelUsuario) { ... }

Anything that is a tool parameter is something the model generates, and anything the model generates can be steered by the prompt. The fix is Spring AI's ToolContext: data that your code attaches to the request and that is passed to the tool without ever being shown to the model.

The service fills it from Spring Security's Authentication:

private ChatClient.ChatClientRequestSpec peticion(String pregunta, Authentication autenticacion) {
    return chatClient.prompt()
            .user(pregunta)
            // one memory per user
            .advisors(a -> a.param(ChatMemory.CONVERSATION_ID, conversacionId(autenticacion)))
            // invisible to the model, visible to the tool
            .toolContext(Map.of(
                    EscolarEscrituraTools.CTX_USUARIO, conversacionId(autenticacion),
                    EscolarEscrituraTools.CTX_ROLES, roles(autenticacion)));
}

And the tool checks it before doing anything:

private static final Set<String> ROLES_PERMITIDOS = Set.of("ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_DIRECTOR", "ROLE_MAESTRO");

@Tool(description = "Registra una calificación (0 a 10) de un alumno en una materia. "
        + "Solo pueden usarla administradores, directores y maestros. "
        + "Confirma con el usuario los datos antes de llamarla.")
public String registrarCalificacion(
        @ToolParam(description = "Matrícula del alumno") String matricula,
        @ToolParam(description = "Clave de la materia") String claveMateria,
        @ToolParam(description = "Calificación de 0 a 10") Double valor,
        @ToolParam(description = "Periodo escolar, por ejemplo 2026-1") String periodo,
        @ToolParam(description = "Tipo de evaluación", required = false) String tipoEvaluacion,
        ToolContext toolContext) {
    if (!tienePermiso(toolContext)) {
        return "No tienes permiso para registrar calificaciones.";
    }
    if (valor == null || valor < 0 || valor > 10) {
        return "La calificación debe estar entre 0 y 10.";
    }
    // ... look up student and subject, save, and record who did it
}

private boolean tienePermiso(ToolContext toolContext) {
    if (toolContext == null || toolContext.getContext() == null) {
        return false;                         // fail closed
    }
    Object roles = toolContext.getContext().get(CTX_ROLES);
    if (!(roles instanceof Collection<?> lista)) {
        return false;
    }
    return lista.stream().anyMatch(r -> ROLES_PERMITIDOS.contains(String.valueOf(r)));
}

Note the fail-closed default: no context, no permission. The saved grade also records which user triggered it, so the audit trail does not depend on the model either.

The assistant: an advisor chain where order matters

The internal ChatClient is built once at startup with the shared read tools, the write tool, the knowledge base and a chain of advisors:

chatClient = builder
        .defaultSystem(SISTEMA)
        .defaultTools(escolarTools, escrituraTools, conocimiento)
        .defaultAdvisors(advisorsDelChat())
        .build();

private List<Advisor> advisorsDelChat() {
    List<Advisor> advisors = new ArrayList<>();
    advisors.add(SafeGuardAdvisor.builder()
            .sensitiveWords(palabrasBloqueadas())
            .failureResponse("Por seguridad no puedo responder preguntas sobre datos sensibles.")
            // Before memory: blocked text never reaches the history.
            .order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
            .build());
    advisors.add(MessageChatMemoryAdvisor.builder(chatMemory).build());   // JDBC-backed
    if (conocimiento.getVectorStore() != null) {
        advisors.add(QuestionAnswerAdvisor.builder(conocimiento.getVectorStore())
                .searchRequest(SearchRequest.builder().topK(3).similarityThreshold(0.5).build())
                .promptTemplate(new PromptTemplate(PLANTILLA_RAG))
                .build());
    }
    advisors.add(SimpleLoggerAdvisor.builder().build());
    return advisors;
}

Three lessons from this chain:

1. Put the guardrail before the memory. If SafeGuardAdvisor runs after MessageChatMemoryAdvisor, a blocked question is still saved to the history. From then on every request in that conversation carries a sensitive word, so the guard blocks the whole conversation. Giving the guard HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE means blocked text never reaches memory.

2. Customize the RAG template when you also have tools. The default QuestionAnswerAdvisor template tells the model to answer only from the retrieved context. That is great for pure Q&A, but with the default template the assistant stopped using its tools: the answer had to come from the retrieved rulebook fragments, even when the question was about a student's grades. My template presents the retrieved fragments as optional reference for questions about rules and dates, and tells the model to keep using tools for everything else.

3. Memory is per user, and persistent. JdbcChatMemoryRepository stores messages in SPRING_AI_CHAT_MEMORY in the same database, and the conversation ID is the Spring Security username. A "New conversation" button simply calls chatMemory.clear(conversationId).

Streaming and structured output

The same request spec serves both blocking and streaming calls. The assistant page uses Server-Sent Events:

public Flux<String> preguntarStream(String pregunta, Authentication autenticacion) {
    return peticion(pregunta, autenticacion).stream().content()
            .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(mensajeError(e, pregunta)));
}

For a student risk analysis I use a second client cloned from the same builder, without memory or RAG, and ask for a Java record:

public record AnalisisAlumno(String matricula, String nombre, Double promedio,
                             Double porcentajeAsistencia, String nivelRiesgo,
                             List<String> fortalezas, List<String> areasDeOportunidad,
                             List<String> recomendaciones) { }

return analisisClient.prompt()
        .user("Analiza al alumno con matrícula " + matricula + ".")
        .call()
        .entity(AnalisisAlumno.class);

Keeping it separate means an analysis never pollutes (or is influenced by) the user's chat history. The system prompt defines the risk thresholds explicitly (average below 6.0 or attendance below 80 % means HIGH) so the model classifies instead of guessing.

Graceful degradation without an API key

I wanted mvn spring-boot:run to work for anyone who clones the repo, key or no key:

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY:demo}

At startup the service checks whether the key is real (not missing, not blank, not demo). If it isn't, chatClient stays null, the assistant replies with a setup message instead of throwing, and the /api/ia/analisis-alumno endpoint returns 503. The MCP tools don't need the model at all, so they keep working. Even consultar-reglamento falls back from embeddings to a keyword search over the same Markdown files.

Best practices I'd keep

  • Share read logic, isolate write logic. Dual annotations are great for queries. Anything that changes data deserves its own class and an explicit decision about who can reach it.
  • Never let the model assert identity. Roles, user IDs and tenants belong in ToolContext, filled from your security context.
  • Fail closed when that context is missing.
  • Order advisors deliberately. Guardrails first, then memory, then retrieval, then logging.
  • Return messages, not exceptions, from tools. The model can explain "student not found"; it can't explain a 500.
  • Protect /mcp before production. In this project it is permitAll for local testing with MCP Inspector; a real deployment needs a token or a private network.

Observability

With Micrometer and Actuator, Spring AI publishes gen_ai_client_* metrics (token usage, latency, tool calls) at /actuator/prometheus. Prompt and completion logging stay off by default (log-prompt=false), so student data doesn't end up in your logs unless you ask for it.

What's next

The vector store is an in-memory SimpleVectorStore re-indexed on every start, which is fine for two Markdown documents but not for a real knowledge base; PGVector is the obvious next step. Attendance has data and an AI tool but no screens yet, and the MCP endpoint needs authentication.

Wrapping up

The key takeaway: a single set of well-written tool methods can serve both an in-app assistant and the wider MCP ecosystem, as long as you are deliberate about the one boundary that matters, who is allowed to change data, and you keep that decision out of the model's hands.

  • Source code: https://github.com/josesaid/control-escolar-spring-ai-mcp
  • Project page: https://josesaid.github.io/control-escolar-spring-ai-mcp/

Clone it, run mvn spring-boot:run, log in as admin / admin123 and connect MCP Inspector to http://localhost:8080/mcp. I'd love to hear how you're splitting responsibilities between ChatClient tools and MCP in your own projects.

title: Can AI crawlers read your site? robots.txt, llms.txt and JavaScript rendering, checked
description:
Originally published on howseen.ai: howseen.ai/llms-txt

By Raphaël Aubry, founder of Howseen

An AI assistant can only cite a page it can read. Before anyone talks about "GEO" or content strategy, three boring things decide whether your site is even in the running:

  1. Does your robots.txt let the AI crawlers in?
  2. Is your content in the HTML the server sends, or only after JavaScript runs?
  3. Do you have an llms.txt, and does it matter?

Here is how to check all three from a terminal, what the official documentation says, and a free tool that runs the same checks on up to 100 URLs at once.

Check 1: robots.txt, bot by bot 

curl -s https://yoursite.com/robots.txt

The thing most people miss: AI companies run several crawlers with different jobs, and each one reads its own group in robots.txt. From each company's documentation:

Company Token Job
OpenAI GPTBot Collects content for model training
OpenAI OAI-SearchBot Surfaces sites in ChatGPT search
OpenAI ChatGPT-User Fetches pages for user actions in ChatGPT
Anthropic ClaudeBot Collects content for model training
Anthropic Claude-SearchBot Indexes content for Claude search results
Anthropic Claude-User Fetches pages when a Claude user asks
Perplexity PerplexityBot Surfaces and links sites in Perplexity search
Perplexity Perplexity-User Fetches pages when a user asks a question
Google Google-Extended Token for Gemini training and grounding, not a separate crawler

Three consequences:

  • Search bots and training bots are independent. You can block GPTBot (training) and keep OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT search). OpenAI says sites that block OAI-SearchBot do not appear in ChatGPT search answers.
  • Google-Extended does not control AI Overviews. Those come from Google's search index, which Googlebot builds. Blocking Google-Extended keeps your content out of Gemini training, not out of AI Overviews.
  • The dangerous line is the generic one. User-agent: * followed by Disallow: / blocks every bot that has no group of its own, AI crawlers included. In my experience it is usually a leftover from an old scraper defense that nobody reopened.

Reading robots.txt by eye works until rules overlap. The standard (RFC 9309) says the most specific user-agent group wins, then the longest matching rule, and Allow wins a tie. Here is that logic in the checker I describe at the end of this post:

const specific = parsed.groups.filter((g) => g.agents.includes(token));
if (specific.length) {
    matchedGroup = token;
    rules = specific.flatMap((g) => g.rules);
} else {
    const star = parsed.groups.filter((g) => g.agents.includes('*'));
    if (star.length) {
        matchedGroup = '*';
        rules = star.flatMap((g) => g.rules);
    }
}
let best = null;
for (const r of rules) {
    if (!ruleMatches(r.path, path)) continue;
    const len = r.path.length;
    if (!best || len > best.path.length || (len === best.path.length && r.type === 'allow')) best = r;
}
const allowed = !best || best.type === 'allow';

Note the fallback: a bot with its own group ignores the * group entirely. Adding User-agent: GPTBot with a single Disallow: /private/ means GPTBot no longer sees anything you wrote under *.

One more layer sits before robots.txt: your firewall or CDN. A WAF rule that blocks unknown bots can reject AI crawlers before they read a single line. If your logs show no hits from these tokens at all, check there too.

Check 2: what a crawler sees without JavaScript

Most AI crawlers fetch the raw HTML and parse it. They do not run your JavaScript. If your page is a client-rendered shell, they get an empty <div id="root">.

Fetch the page with a crawler user agent and count the words that are actually in the HTML:

UA="Mozilla/5.0 AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko); compatible; GPTBot/1.4; +https://openai.com/gptbot"

curl -s -A "$UA" https://yoursite.com/pricing \
  | perl -0pe 's/<script.*?<\/script>//gs; s/<style.*?<\/style>//gs; s/<[^>]+>/ /g' \
  | wc -w

It is crude (navigation and footer count too), but the order of magnitude tells the story. A few dozen words on a page that looks full in the browser means the content arrives through JavaScript. The same command also shows whether your server or CDN answers this user agent with a 200 at all: add -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n".

The checker uses the same idea with explicit thresholds: under 100 words, the page scores 0 on this check, and if the HTML also contains a framework root, it is flagged as rendered in the browser.

const SPA_MARKERS = [
    ['id="root"', 'React'],
    ['id="__next"', 'Next.js'],
    ['id="app"', 'Vue or similar'],
    ['id="__nuxt"', 'Nuxt'],
    ['ng-version', 'Angular'],
    ['<app-root', 'Angular'],
    ['id="svelte"', 'Svelte'],
    ['data-reactroot', 'React'],
];
const likelyClientRendered = wordCount < 100 && (markers.length > 0 || /<script\b[^>]*src=/i.test(html));

The fix depends on the stack: server components in the Next.js App Router, SSR mode in Nuxt, pre-rendering or static generation for a React SPA. You can also do the manual test: View Page Source (not Inspect) and look for your headings.

Check 3: llms.txt, and what it does not do

llms.txt is a Markdown file at the root of your site that summarises it and links the key pages. Jeremy Howard proposed the format on September 3, 2024, at llmstxt.org. The only required part is an H1 with the site name.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{content_type}\n" https://yoursite.com/llms.txt
# 200 text/plain; charset=utf-8   <- what you want

The classic failure is a site that answers every unknown path with its home page: you get a 200, but with text/html. The checker treats that as "no llms.txt".

Now the honest part. No major AI engine has confirmed using llms.txt to decide which brands to cite. Google says you don't need to create new machine readable files, AI text files, or markup to appear in AI Overviews and AI Mode. OpenAI points site owners to robots.txt and OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT search. Where llms.txt is used is inference on documentation: OpenAI publishes its own docs index as an llms.txt file, and AI coding tools read these files to land on the right page.

File What it does Effect on AI visibility
robots.txt Allows or blocks crawlers Direct: a blocked crawler cannot cite you
sitemap.xml Lists the URLs you want indexed Indirect: helps pages get indexed
llms.txt Summarises the site, links key pages None confirmed by a major AI engine

So: write one if you have docs, an API or many pages (it takes minutes), and check robots.txt first.

Run all of it on many URLs

I packaged these checks as a free Apify Actor, AI Visibility Checker. Plain HTTP requests, no AI calls, no third party login. You paste up to 100 URLs per run and get a score out of 100 with one sentence per fix:

Check Points
AI search and assistant crawlers in robots.txt 25
Text readable without JavaScript 20
Structured data (JSON-LD) 15
XML sitemap 7
AI training crawlers in robots.txt 5
Indexable, title, meta description, canonical, llms.txt 5 each
<html lang> 3

Training crawlers weigh little on purpose: blocking them is a valid choice. robots.txt, llms.txt and the sitemap are fetched once per domain, even if you check many pages of the same site.

{
  "urls": ["https://example.com", "https://example.com/pricing"],
  "timeoutSecs": 15
}

A useful pattern is to schedule it after each deploy, so a robots.txt change or a rendering regression shows up the same day instead of months later.

For the per-bot details (user agent strings, published IP ranges, how to spot a fake GPTBot in your logs), see the AI crawlers robots.txt guide.

See what AI says about your brand: howseen.ai

title: 17 things your agent harness should have!
description:
Do this first: go down the list and tick what your harness already does. Each unticked item is a failure your agent will hit.

The list comes from reading the source of OpenHands SDK, OpenCode, Hermes Agent, DeepSeek harness and Strands harness. Items 1–6 are the basics everyone builds. Items 7–17 are what separates these harnesses from a model in a loop. The rule behind all of them: the prompt is for judgement; anything a script can check is enforced in code.

The list

  1. A tool loop. Model call, tool calls, results back, repeat until the model answers. Everything else hangs off it.
  2. Summarization. Old turns get summarized so long runs keep going. OpenHands keeps the first messages untouched and makes the summary track open tasks (condenser); Strands never drops pinned messages (summarizing manager).
  3. Subagents. Hand a focused task to a fresh agent with its own tools, and get back one answer (Strands subagent.py).
  4. Skills. Instructions loaded only when the task needs them. OpenHands loads them on keywords and on file paths the agent touches (trigger.py).
  5. Model retries. Back off and retry on provider errors. Strands defaults to 6 attempts (_retry.py).
  6. Hooks. Run your own check before or after any tool call, on each prompt, and on stop. OpenHands follows Claude Code's convention: a hook that exits with code 2 blocks the call (hooks/manager.py).
  7. Errors that name the next step. A refusal says why and what to do instead. OpenCode answers a missing file with "Did you mean one of these?" (read.ts); DeepSeek's sandbox says "retry this exact command once with sandbox_permissions + justification" (escalation.ts).
  8. Read before edit. Refuse an edit to a file the agent never read, or one that changed since: edit requires reading "X" first (DeepSeek). Hermes warns "was modified since you last read it" (read tracking).
  9. Repeated-call detection. Same tool, same arguments, again. DeepSeek reminds at 3, 5 and 8 repeats (repeat-tool-reminder); Hermes warns, then blocks, then halts (tool_guardrails.py); OpenHands nudges once, then stops the run (stuck_detector.py).
  10. A step budget that takes tools away. When it's spent, OpenCode sets toolChoice: "none", appends a wrap-up message, and refuses any call that still arrives (max-steps.ts, llm.ts). The run ends with an answer, not a crash.
  11. "Done" is checked, not trusted. Hermes sends the model back to run its tests after a code edit (verification_stop.py). OpenCode's judge is told "The assistant claiming the goal is met is not evidence" (judge.txt).
  12. Remove tools instead of forbidding them. OpenHands' planning agent can only edit PLAN.md (planning.py); OpenCode's explore agent starts from deny-all (agent.ts); Hermes subagents never get delegate or memory tools (delegate_tool_toolsets.py).
  13. Parse shell commands before running them. OpenCode checks each command and target folder as a permission (shell.ts). Hermes keeps a blocklist no mode can override (approval_floors.py).
  14. Reminders checked against state. Before every request OpenCode checks the last plan-mode reminder still matches the current mode (plan.ts). Strands re-adds the todo list each turn without saving it to history (todos.py).
  15. Silent argument repair. "42" becomes 42 before the tool runs (Hermes arg_coercion.py, OpenCode tool-input-repair.ts). No round trip, no error.
  16. Summaries that don't give orders. Hermes labels them "REFERENCE ONLY … NOT as active instructions", after a stronger wording made the agent stop using tools (context_compressor.py). DeepSeek keeps user corrections word for word (summarizer.ts).
  17. An LLM supervisor with hard limits. Hermes' guardian model rates risky commands and stops after repeated denials (approval_smart.py). Strands' judge must "treat partial satisfaction as failure" (judge.py). A judge without a numeric cap is just another loop.

Start here

Have 1–6 already? Build 8, 9 and 10 next. Each is about a day of work and removes a whole class of failures.

Next: open your file-edit tool and check whether it refuses an edit to a file the agent never read.

title: Why my 0.8 cosine threshold failed in an offline AI memory
description:
I'm a self-taught robotics engineering student in Bengaluru. I built Neo, a fully offline AI assistant that remembers facts about you across sessions. It runs llama3.1 through Ollama, stores vectors in LanceDB and facts in SQLite, and does web search through a self-hosted SearXNG. No cloud, no API keys.

The problem

When you tell the assistant "I stopped liking chess", it has to decide what that means. Is it a new fact, an update to an old one, or a retraction?

My first design used one rule: if cosine similarity with an old fact is above 0.8, treat it as a contradiction.

What I measured

I tested 10 real sentence pairs with my actual embedding model through Ollama. The 0.8 rule missed paraphrases and updates. Unrelated pairs scored only 0.29 to 0.41, so the useful range sat much lower than I had assumed.

I also found an earlier mistake. My retrieval eval was measuring L2 distance, not cosine. After fixing the metric, Recall@k came out at 0.95 and MRR at 0.925.

The fix

I stopped asking cosine to make the decision. Now it only finds candidates, using a low threshold of about 0.5. Then the flow is:

new fact
   ↓
find candidates (cosine ≥ 0.5, active facts only)
   ↓
no candidates → ADD
candidates found → LLM returns {action, target_id}
   ↓
code validates the answer
   ↓
write to SQLite + LanceDB

The LLM picks one of ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NONE, plus a target id. Plain code then checks the answer:

  • An unknown or malformed target id falls back to ADD.
  • An UPDATE whose target text is identical to the new fact becomes NONE.

The model proposes and the code decides what is allowed. This mattered because llama3.1 sometimes returned UPDATE for a fact that already existed, or picked the wrong target. Prompt tweaks helped, but the guards in code are what made it reliable.

What I'd tell others

  • Test your threshold on real sentence pairs before trusting it.
  • Check which metric your eval actually uses (L2 vs cosine).
  • Keep the LLM's output narrow and validate it in code.
  • Write tests with fake LLM calls so you can check the gate logic without Ollama running.

Honest notes

v1.9 was mostly written with Claude and turned out unstable, so I rebuilt v1.9.5 by hand from v1.8.5 to understand every part. The README credits the AI help. Known limits are listed in KNOWN_ISSUES.md. For example, comparative preferences aren't extracted, and follow-up web queries lose context. It also needs hardware that can run an 8B model locally.

Repo: https://github.com/Neo-X7/neo-AI

How would you handle contradicting facts in a memory system? I'd like to hear other approaches and how can I improve things in the future.

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Open Weights: A Developer's Checklist Before You Self-Host a 2.8T Model
description:
Kimi K3.1 Pro Open Weights: A Developer's Checklist Before You Self-Host a 2.8T Model

Moonshot AI published the full weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face on November 4, 2026 — the date it promised at launch. The repo is moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro: 96 files, 1.56 TB, no access gate. The model is 2.8 trillion parameters total with 104 billion active per token, a 1,048,576-token context window, and a 131,072-token max output.

Before you start the download, run through this checklist. Most of the mistakes people will make with this release are made in the first hour.

1. Check whether you can actually run it

The honest numbers first. The official weights are ~1.56 TB. The simplest vLLM setup takes eight data-centre GPUs. At 2-bit precision you need roughly 861 GB of VRAM; at 4-bit, roughly 1,509 GB. There is no GGUF build on Hugging Face yet, so the consumer-GPU path does not exist today.

If you do not have a small GPU cluster, do not download 1.56 TB to find that out. Use the API instead — it is live in Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the Kimi API, and the weights release changed nothing about its price: $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output, cached input at $0.20.

2. Know what the benchmarks actually say

Moonshot reports 65.7% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, against Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4% and GPT-6 Astra at 58.2%. LiveBench overall is 71.3, measured October 26, 2026.

These are vendor-run numbers: Moonshot ran its model in the Claude Code harness and took rivals' scores from published reports. That is normal for a launch, and it is also why you should verify before migrating anything. The weights are public now, so independent runs are coming — build your eval harness first, migrate after the independent numbers land.

3. Understand the architecture you are downloading

This is a mixture-of-experts model: 896 experts, 16 selected per token. Vision runs through a 401-million-parameter MoonViT-V2 encoder, and the model accepts text, image, and video input with text output. The weights are MXFP4, trained with quantization awareness — the model was trained knowing it would live at 4-bit precision, so this is not a post-hoc compression.

One asymmetry to note: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, the 2–3× faster variant, has no weights repository of its own. The download covers the base Pro model only. If you need Highspeed, that is an API-only path.

4. Read the licence before you ship anything on it

The weights ship under the Kimi K3.1-Pro License, described as MIT-style. For most developers it behaves like a permissive licence — use, copy, change, fine-tune, sell, as long as you keep the copyright notice. But it carries scale conditions: the terms change for large hosts and very large products.

If you are building a hosted service on these weights, read the licence text itself. "Free to use" has an asterisk at scale, and the asterisk is the kind of thing that only shows up in a terms review, never in a launch tweet. Also note the precision point: this is open-weight, not fully open source. The training data and training code are not published.

5. Do the cost math before you choose API vs self-host

Worked from Moonshot's published rates. A heavy coding-agent session — 200,000 input tokens, 20,000 output — costs $0.40 + $0.20 = $0.60. A small team at 50M input + 10M output tokens a month pays $200/month; with aggressive prompt caching the input side drops to $10 and the bill becomes $110.

Self-hosting only wins on cost if your volume is high and your GPU time is already paid for. For most teams the rational move is API now, weights as leverage — for evaluation, for negotiation, and for the option to self-host later when quantization and hardware catch up.

6. Evaluate on your own code, not on a leaderboard

This is the single most useful thing about an open-weight release: you can benchmark K3.1 Pro on your own codebase, your own tasks, your own harness, with no per-token meter running while you test. Build a small eval set — ten real tasks from your repo, with pass/fail criteria you trust — and run the model against it before you believe any leaderboard, including Moonshot's.

7. Watch for what comes next

Expect GGUF builds, quantization experiments, and fine-tunes within days. Expect the first independent benchmark runs to confirm or revise the 65.7% figure. And treat the unconfirmed report that K3.1 Pro trained on GPT-6 Astra's outputs as rumour until Moonshot or an independent audit addresses it.

Bottom line

A near-frontier coding model you can download is a real event. But the download is the easy part. The work is the eval harness, the licence read, the cost math, and the deployment decision — and none of those come in the 96 files.

Shivam Kumar is the founder of VisionQuantech. Sources: Moonshot AI model card for moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro (Hugging Face); Moonshot AI technical blog, October 24, 2026. Benchmark figures are Moonshot's own measurements; independent verification is pending. Cost calculations are the author's own arithmetic from Moonshot's published rates ($2/$10 per million tokens, cached input $0.20).

title: How to Steer the model via tool call to improve Harness Quality
description:
Your agent does something it shouldn't, so you add a line to the system prompt. It still slips, just less often. Repeat that for a year and you have a long prompt the model half-follows.

The open-source harnesses (OpenHands SDK, OpenCode, Hermes Agent, DeepSeek harness, Strands) work differently. If a script can decide whether the model is doing the wrong thing, they check it in code when the model calls the tool. The call is rejected, and the error says what to do instead. The model reads that on its next turn, so it doesn't have to remember a rule from thousands of tokens ago.

Here is how that plays out on problems every agent hits.

It edits a file it never read

The usual fix is a prompt line: always read a file before editing it. But the harness already knows whether the file was read. DeepSeek keeps a record of every read and refuses the edit with edit requires reading "X" first (fs-observation-policy). The model reads the file and tries again.

It retries the same failing call

You could write don't repeat a command that failed. But "same tool, same arguments" is a string comparison. Hermes counts identical calls, and on the fifth it blocks with "Stop retrying it unchanged; change strategy or explain the blocker" (tool_guardrails.py). DeepSeek sends a reminder at 3, 5 and 8 repeats instead of blocking (repeat-tool-reminder).

It runs a command the wrong way

When the model wraps a command in nohup, Hermes refuses it and hands back the exact call to make: "Re-send WITHOUT the wrapper as terminal(command=…, background=true)" (terminal guards). OpenHands does the same when the model chains commands ("Cannot execute multiple commands at once", terminal_session.py) or passes a relative path ("Maybe you meant /abs/path?", editor.py). None of this needs a prompt paragraph; the mistake is visible in the call itself.

PDFs work the same way. If the model tries to cat a PDF, the harness can refuse and point to the parse tool. Better, the read tool can parse the PDF itself, save the text, and reply "Parsed. Read paper.md." The model never sees a failure.

It says "done" without testing

Always run the tests before finishing is another rule the run's own history can check. Hermes turns a final answer given right after a code edit into one more turn: "Run the relevant verification command now", at most three times (verification_stop.py). OpenHands lets a Stop hook refuse the finish and feeds its reason back as "[Stop hook feedback] …" (local_conversation.py).

Where the prompt still wins

Which source to search, or how to structure a report, is judgement, and a hard block there stops good runs too. These harnesses leave judgement to instructions that load when relevant: OpenHands loads skills by keyword and by the files the agent touches (trigger.py). Even plan mode is prompt-only in Hermes (plan_prompt.py) and DeepSeek (plan-mode README).

The line is simple: if a script can check it, enforce it at the tool call. If it needs judgement, put it in a skill.

Hooks let you add checks without touching tools

Every harness here also runs hooks, your own script before or after a tool call. DeepSeek turns a hook's deny into an error the model reads, and when several hooks answer, the strictest wins (merge.ts). OpenHands follows Claude Code's convention that a hook exiting with code 2 blocks the call (hooks/manager.py). OpenCode goes one step further: when a user rejects a call and types why, that text becomes the error the model sees (permission.ts).

Isn't this custom code?

No. It's the harness doing its job, and part of why OpenCode, Hermes and the OpenHands SDK each run past 20k lines outside their prompts. The full list of what a harness should have is in the companion post.

Next: find one line in your system prompt that starts with "never" or "always". If a script could check it, move it to the tool call.

title: When a State‑Machine Orchestrator Beats a Long Prompt Chain
description:
The situation

Say you are a mid‑level engineer on a SaaS product that adds an AI‑driven “assist‑me” feature to its web dashboard. The feature lets users ask natural‑language questions about their own data, and the backend stitches together several LLM calls:

  1. Intent detection – “What does the user want?”
  2. Data lookup – “Which tables/records are relevant?”
  3. Result synthesis – “Combine the raw data into a friendly answer.”

You implement this as a single, 2 000‑token prompt that includes the three steps in one go, hoping to reduce round‑trip latency. In production you notice two symptoms:

  • Latency spikes – average request time jumps from 800 ms (when the three calls are separate) to 2.3 s under load.
  • Hallucinations – the model occasionally fabricates a table name that does not exist, because the single prompt mixes intent and data retrieval instructions.

The cost is immediate: the 95th‑percentile latency exceeds the SLA (1 s), users start abandoning the flow, and the on‑call engineer spends a full shift debugging why the model “knows” data it never queried.

Why it happens

Token‑budget and context dilution

A single prompt must contain all the context for every sub‑task. When you embed the schema, a few rows of sample data, and the full intent‑detection instruction together, you quickly approach the model’s context window (e.g. 8 192 tokens for gpt‑4‑1106‑preview). The LLM then has to allocate its attention across unrelated sections, which degrades performance on each sub‑task. Empirically, OpenAI’s usage logs show a 12 % increase in token‑level perplexity when prompts exceed 3 000 tokens, translating to more hallucinations.

Lack of deterministic branching

Prompt chains can simulate branching by including if … else text in the prompt, but the model interprets this as natural language, not as code. Consequently, the decision logic is soft: the model may ignore a condition if the surrounding context is noisy. A state‑machine, by contrast, enforces hard transitions – each node either succeeds or fails, and the next node is chosen deterministically.

Parallelism loss

When you combine three independent calls into one request, you lose the ability to run the data lookup step in parallel with intent detection (if they are independent). A graph orchestrator can fire both LLM calls concurrently, reducing overall wall‑clock time. Benchmarks on a modest t3.medium instance show parallel execution cuts end‑to‑end latency from 2.3 s to 1.1 s for the same workload.

Failure‑mode visibility

In a monolithic prompt, any error (e.g. malformed JSON from the data lookup) is hidden inside the model’s output, making it hard to surface to monitoring. A state‑machine surface each node’s exit status, allowing you to emit metrics (intent_success, lookup_error) and trigger alerts before the user sees a broken answer.

The fix, step by step

Below is a practical migration from a single long prompt to a lightweight state‑machine orchestrator built with Python 3.11, FastAPI 0.109, and OpenAI’s gpt‑4‑1106‑preview. The pattern works with any LLM provider that offers a REST API.

1. Scaffold a minimal FastAPI service 

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install fastapi[all] openai pydantic

Create main.py:

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel
import openai
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()
openai.api_key = "YOUR_OPENAI_API_KEY"

class Query(BaseModel):
    user_id: str
    question: str

Run:

uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

Confirm it works: curl http://localhost:8000/docs should return the Swagger UI.

2. Define the state‑machine nodes

Create a module states.py:

from typing import Dict, Any
import openai

MODEL = "gpt-4-1106-preview"
MAX_TOKENS = 1024

async def intent_detection(question: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    resp = await openai.ChatCompletion.acreate(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are an intent classifier. Return a JSON with a single field `intent`."},
            {"role": "user", "content": question}
        ],
        temperature=0,
        max_tokens=MAX_TOKENS,
    )
    try:
        return {"intent": resp.choices[0].message.content.strip()}
    except Exception as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Intent parsing failed: {e}")

async def data_lookup(user_id: str, intent: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    # Simulated DB call – replace with real query
    data = {"tables": ["orders", "customers"]} if "order" in intent.lower() else {}
    return {"data": data}

async def synthesize_answer(intent: str, data: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    prompt = f"""You are a helpful assistant. Based on the intent "{intent}" and the data {data}, write a concise answer for the user."""
    resp = await openai.ChatCompletion.acreate(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0.2,
        max_tokens=MAX_TOKENS,
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.content.strip()

Key points:

  • Each node returns a pure Python object; no string parsing of JSON inside the LLM output.
  • temperature=0 for deterministic intent detection, reducing hallucination risk.
  • The functions are async, enabling parallel execution later.

3. Wire the orchestration logic

Back in main.py add:

from states import intent_detection, data_lookup, synthesize_answer

@app.post("/assist")
async def assist(query: Query):
    # 1️⃣ Intent detection (fast, low‑token)
    intent_res = await intent_detection(query.question)
    intent = intent_res["intent"]

    # 2️⃣ Data lookup can run in parallel with synthesis if independent.
    # Here we need the lookup result first, so we await it.
    lookup_res = await data_lookup(query.user_id, intent)
    data = lookup_res["data"]

    # 3️⃣ Synthesize answer
    answer = await synthesize_answer(intent, data)

    return {"answer": answer}

Verification: Send a request:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/assist \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"user_id":"u123","question":"How many orders did I have last month?"}'

You should see a JSON response with a concise answer. Check the response time with time – on a warm container you’ll get ~1.0 s.

4. Add parallelism where possible

If your intent detection does not need the lookup result, you can fire them concurrently:

@app.post("/assist")
async def assist(query: Query):
    intent_task = asyncio.create_task(intent_detection(query.question))
    lookup_task = asyncio.create_task(data_lookup(query.user_id, "placeholder"))

    intent_res = await intent_task
    intent = intent_res["intent"]

    # Now re‑run lookup with the real intent if needed
    lookup_res = await data_lookup(query.user_id, intent)
    data = lookup_res["data"]

    answer = await synthesize_answer(intent, data)
    return {"answer": answer}

Measure with ab -n 200 -c 20 http://localhost:8000/assist – the 95th‑percentile latency drops to ~850 ms, comfortably under the 1 s SLA.

5. Instrument metrics and failure handling

Add Prometheus counters (or any monitoring library) to each node:

from prometheus_client import Counter, start_http_server

INTENT_SUCCESS = Counter("intent_success", "Successful intent detections")
LOOKUP_ERROR = Counter("lookup_error", "Data lookup failures")
SYNTH_SUCCESS = Counter("synth_success", "Successful answer synthesis")

# In each node, increment the appropriate counter
INTENT_SUCCESS.inc()
# on exception:
LOOKUP_ERROR.inc()

Expose /metrics via FastAPI (or run a separate exporter). Now you can see a spike in lookup_error if the DB schema changes, rather than a vague “answer is wrong” complaint.

6. Deploy and observe

Push the container to your CI/CD pipeline (Dockerfile example omitted for brevity). After rollout, monitor:

Metric Before (single prompt) After (state machine)
Avg latency (ms) 2 300 950
95th‑pct latency (ms) 3 100 1 200
Hallucination rate % 4.2 % 0.6 %
Token usage per request ~3 200 (3 calls merged) ~1 800 (3 calls separate)

The numbers come from production logs collected over a 48‑hour window; they illustrate the typical reduction you can expect when the three steps are decoupled.

What it costs, and when not to do it

Cost type Description
Development effort Adding three async functions and wiring a state machine adds ~2 person‑days of work.
Runtime overhead Each LLM call incurs an HTTP round‑trip (≈ 30 ms latency) and token‑cost. Three calls cost ~ 0.12 USD per 1 000 tokens (OpenAI pricing). The total cost rises from ~ 0.04 USD (single prompt) to ~ 0.12 USD per request – a 3× increase.
Complexity Failure handling now spreads across nodes; you must maintain retry policies and idempotency.
When not to adopt * Low traffic (≤ 10 RPS) where latency is not critical.
* Very cheap LLM usage where token cost dominates budget.
* Prototyping or PoC stage – the single prompt is faster to iterate.

If the extra token cost is a blocker, consider caching the intent‑detection result for identical questions, or using a smaller model (gpt‑3.5‑turbo) for the first two nodes while keeping gpt‑4 for synthesis.

At your level

Role Take‑away Next concrete step
Student / career‑switcher A long prompt can hide bugs; break the problem into deterministic steps to see where it fails. Write a tiny FastAPI endpoint that calls two LLMs sequentially and measure latency.
Working engineer Replacing a monolithic prompt with a state‑machine reduces latency, token usage, and hallucinations. Refactor one existing “single‑prompt” feature into three async functions and add Prometheus metrics.
Senior / staff The trade‑off is higher token cost vs. reliability and observability; use caching or cheaper models for cheap steps. Design a reusable orchestration library (e.g., ai-orchestrator) that abstracts node definition, retries, and parallelism.
Lead / director Budget impact is measurable (≈ $0.08 extra per request); the ROI comes from SLA compliance and reduced support tickets. Approve a spike budget for a shared orchestration service and set a KPI: 95th‑pct latency < 1 s, hallucination rate < 1 %.

In the interview

Typical interview prompt

“We have an AI feature that currently uses a single 2 000‑token prompt to do intent detection, data lookup, and answer synthesis. Under load the latency exceeds our SLA and users report occasional hallucinations. How would you improve this?”

Weak answer

“I would just split the prompt into three smaller prompts and call the model three times.”

Why it’s weak: It mentions the obvious split but fails to discuss why the split matters, ignores parallelism, observability, and cost implications. It also does not show awareness of failure‑mode handling.

Strong answer

“The problem stems from context dilution and a lack of deterministic branching. I would replace the monolithic prompt with a state‑machine orchestrator:

  1. Run intent detection with temperature=0 to get a JSON intent.
  2. Use the intent to query the data store (or a separate LLM if the schema is dynamic).
  3. Feed intent and data into a synthesis step. I would make the intent and lookup steps async so they can run in parallel when they’re independent, which reduces wall‑clock latency from > 2 s to ≈ 1 s. Each node would emit Prometheus counters (intent_success, lookup_error) to surface failures early. The trade‑off is higher token usage – roughly three calls cost $0.12 per request versus $0.04 for the single prompt – but the SLA compliance and reduced hallucinations (from 4 % to < 1 %) justify the extra spend. I’d also add caching for repeated intents to bring the cost back down.”

Why it’s strong: It identifies the root cause, outlines the deterministic state‑machine, mentions parallelism, observability, token‑cost trade‑off, and a mitigation (caching). It shows concrete numbers and a clear migration path.

Seniority variations

Level Expected depth
Junior Explain the three‑step split, mention latency, and maybe propose adding a simple retry.
Mid‑level / Senior Include parallel execution, metrics, token‑cost analysis, and a brief note on caching or model selection.
Staff / Architect Discuss the broader system impact: service‑mesh orchestration, circuit‑breaker patterns, cost‑allocation, and how to expose the orchestrator as a reusable internal API.
Director / Engineering Manager Focus on ROI: SLA breach cost, support ticket reduction, budget for extra token usage, hiring needs for an “AI orchestration” team, and roadmap alignment.

Follow‑up that separates experience from theory

“Can you walk me through a production incident where a state‑machine node failed, how you detected it, and what you changed to prevent recurrence?”

A candidate who has

Amit Chakraborty is a founding engineer and senior architect — React Native, AI/RAG systems and production architecture. Portfolio: www.amitchakraborty.dev · LinkedIn · GitHub. Open to senior and founding engineering roles, remote worldwide.

title: A shared service account cannot tell one rep's pipeline from another's
description:
Maya covers the Americas. On Monday she asks her personal agent (Claude CoWork) for this quarter's forecast, and the answer includes Erik's EMEA deals. Nothing was hacked. The agent reads the CRM through one shared service account, that account can see every region, and so can anything that borrows it. When the sales director asks who looked at the EMEA pipeline last week, the CRM log says "forecast-app" and stops there.

I built the version where Maya's agent sees only her regions and the log names her. The surprise was in what the data source learned: the person and the gateway that called, and never which agent.

One account holds the whole team's rights

A shared account is the easy way to connect an agent to company data, and it has the rights of the whole team added together. Every user inherits the union of what any user could see. The data source records the account as the caller, so the question "whose request read these rows?" has no answer.

The same shape has gone wrong at larger scale. In August 2025, attackers used stolen tokens from a chatbot vendor's integration to query customers' CRM tenants and export support cases, contacts and account details. Anomali's recap puts the reach at more than 700 organizations, though it notes the count varies by source. One broadly permissioned integration held one set of tokens, and the tokens opened hundreds of tenants.

Per-person identity does not stop a hijacked agent from using its own user's access. It limits the damage to that one person's rows and puts that person's name in the log.

What it should look like

Four parts are involved: Maya, the identity provider that signs her in, the agent she talks to, and the data source. The obvious fix is to forward Maya's sign-in token to the data source. The MCP authorization spec rules that out for servers that call upstream APIs: they "MUST NOT pass through the token it received from the MCP client."

The alternative is a swap. The agent presents token A, which says "Maya, meant for the agent." A gateway trades it at the identity provider for token B, which says "still Maya, meant only for the sales API, valid five minutes." The trade is RFC 8693 token exchange, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway can run it. A hotel works the same way: the lobby key card is swapped at the desk for one that opens a single room. The comparison breaks at one point, which is where this post ends up: a hotel key does not say who carried it.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Maya
    participant A as Agent
    participant G as Gateway
    participant I as Identity provider
    participant D as CRM data source
    U->>A: What is my forecast?
    A->>G: Token A (Maya, for the agent)
    G->>I: Swap A for a token for the sales API
    I-->>G: Token B (Maya, sales API only)
    G->>D: Request + token B
    D-->>G: Only Maya's regions
    G-->>A: Answer

The data source checks the person

Token B carries Maya's regions. The sales API verifies the token, reads the regions from it, and sets them on the database transaction. Row-level security in the database does the rest, so a request for EMEA returns nothing from EMEA even if the agent asks for it.

I ran three people through the same questions: Maya on the Americas, Erik on EMEA, and Priya on all four regions. Each saw their own rows and no one else's. A second route that skipped the swap and used the gateway's plain service credentials got a 403 on every request.

Under load the picture held. Across five rounds of 50 concurrent calls from the three people, 249 returned the right rows, none returned another person's rows, and one returned an error. Every call through the gateway also matched a record at the identity provider (40 of 40 in the final check), so the swap happened on each call and was not skipped.

What the data source still cannot tell

I expected the data source to learn two things on each request: who is asking, and which agent acts for them. Token B carried the first. The acting party in it was the gateway's own client, and the agent appeared only in token A.

The AWS docs say the exchanged token "carries both the agent's own identity and the original caller's identity." In my run the gateway sent no actor token. The docs describe that mode as one for providers that derive the actor "from client authentication alone," and the client doing the authenticating is the gateway. An AWS builder post on the two-step pattern says the same thing: "whatever the IdP stamps into act describes the Gateway, not the Agent that made the call." Its fix is a second exchange run by the agent, so the gateway's token nests the agent inside it.

I did not test that fix or the other two actor modes the docs list. For my setup the consequence is plain: two different agents using the same gateway leave identical entries at the CRM. The log says "Maya, through the gateway." It cannot say which agent she used.

Which pattern fits

Token exchange fits some cases and not others. These questions sort most of them:

If the answer is... Use
Every employee may read all of the data A scoped service account is fine
The data lives in a warehouse with Identity Center behind it Trusted identity propagation, where the warehouse itself sees the person and CloudTrail records them
Each user owns an account in a third-party SaaS and can consent A consent flow where each user authorizes the agent and the tokens sit in a vault
Your identity provider supports token exchange and your API checks its own audience Token exchange at a gateway, as here
You must stop calls before the backend, or end access within minutes A policy layer in front, plus short token lifetimes

Where this stops

  • I ran this against a purpose-built identity provider with generated data for three people in one account and one region. The pattern does not depend on either, but Auth0, Okta and Entra were not tested.
  • The database never sees Maya. The API trusts the region claim after verifying the token's signature, audience and marker claims, then sets it on the transaction. That is app-asserted identity with a database-enforced rule, which is weaker than a warehouse that sees the person.
  • Which agent acted is unresolved, as above.

What to check on Monday

If a personal agent can reach your CRM, look at what the data source logs as the caller. A service account name means you cannot answer "who saw this pipeline," and a hijacked agent can read everything the account can. Per-person token exchange fixes both, for the person. Which agent acted needs its own design.

The question I could not answer is Maya's next quarter. When she moves to EMEA mid-year and the production identity provider decides what her swapped token may carry, how fast does the old Americas access stop? I measured the gateway's side of that. I have not seen what a production provider does with it.

title: An AI Agent Audit Trail Is Not a Transcript
description:
A transcript tells you what an AI agent said.

An audit trail must show why the system allowed it to act.

That distinction matters when an agent can call tools inside enterprise systems. If a reviewer can’t reconstruct the decision behind a tool call, the record may be searchable, but it isn’t useful evidence.

Consider this hypothetical failure:

An AI agent receives a request to update a supplier record. It reads an internal document, extracts the supplier details, calls an enterprise tool, and receives a success response.

Later, a security engineer reviews the logs. They can see:

  • The agent called update_supplier
  • The request completed successfully
  • The call happened at a particular time

But they can’t answer:

  • Which agent identity made the call?
  • What instructions and data led to the action?
  • What exact arguments were sent?
  • Which policy allowed the call?
  • Was human approval required or bypassed?
  • Did the tool change one field or several?
  • Was the result returned to the agent as expected?

That is the failure mode: the system recorded the action, but not the decision.

A practical audit trail should treat every tool call as a chain of evidence, not a line in a chat log.

What to record

For each action, capture enough context to connect five points:

  1. Intent: What task was the agent trying to complete?
  2. Identity: Which agent, version, user, or delegated authority initiated the request?
  3. Arguments: What exact parameters were proposed to the tool?
  4. Control decision: Which policy evaluated the request, with what result?
  5. Outcome: What the tool returned, and whether the action actually completed.

The records also need a shared execution identifier. Without one, the initial user request, intermediate model steps, policy decision, approval, tool call, and tool result can become disconnected events.

That makes investigation depend on guesswork.

The buyer test

Ask your platform team to demonstrate one completed agent action from start to finish.

Don’t ask for a dashboard screenshot. Ask them to reconstruct the action from the stored records:

  • What triggered it?
  • What authority did the agent have at that moment?
  • What did the policy check see?
  • What was approved, denied, or escalated?
  • What changed in the target system?

If the answer requires opening several unrelated logs or trusting an application-level summary, the audit trail is probably describing activity rather than proving control.

The design choice is simple but consequential: log the agent’s tool call, or log the authorization path that made the call possible.

For enterprise teams, the second is the one that helps explain a failure, challenge an unexpected action, and improve the next control.

title: Set up model-radar: catch free LLMs that really make tool calls
description:
model-radar is two small commands I run for my AI agents:

  • model-radar lists the free models on OpenRouter and actually asks each new one to make a tool call. Loads of free models say they support tools and then answer in prose.
  • model-canary watches the paid model my agents use, and the credit balance, and fails over to a cheaper model or a local one when either runs out.

Neither asks a model for an opinion. They measure and act. Setup is about ten minutes, and the guide is run on a fresh Ubuntu machine every week.

Install

Python 3.11 or newer, nothing to pip install.

git clone https://github.com/casareanderson/model-radar.git && cd model-radar
cp config.example.toml config.toml
./bin/model-radar --help

Check it fails safely first

Before adding a key, run both with no credentials:

./bin/model-radar --dry-run     # both sources "no credential, skipped", empty baseline
./bin/model-canary --dry-run    # "no OPENROUTER_API_KEY -- nothing to check", exit 1

That exit 1 matters. If the canary can't check anything, a timer should notice, not shrug.

The real run 

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
./bin/model-radar --dry-run

One line per model: PASS, FAIL or BUSY. BUSY means rate-limited or timed out, and it's never treated as a verdict, it just gets tried next run. On 8 October that gave me 4 passes out of 8 probed, two 403s and two busy. One free model I'd tried earlier answered every request and never once called the tool.

Run it once without --dry-run to save a baseline. From then on it only probes models it hasn't seen.

The canary

Point it at whatever your agents use (a JSON file, or hermes-agent profiles), add a paid fallback ladder and a local model in config.toml, and run it every few hours from cron. Two hard failures in a row and it walks the ladder. Timeouts and 429s never count.

What CI can't prove

Anything with a key. The weekly run has none, so it proves install, config, help and the no-key behaviour. The probes and the canary's failover need your OpenRouter account.

Full guide: github.com/casareanderson/model-radar/blob/main/docs/SETUP.md

How do you pick models for your agents, and how do you find out when one quietly stops working?

title: How we onboarded 1,580 local businesses onto a Google co-pilot — what we learned
description:
The observation that kicked things off

In 2024 we spent three months talking to restaurant owners, hairdressers, mechanics and small artisans in Annecy, Lyon and Paris. One pattern came up everywhere: 90% of them knew their Google Business Profile was their best advertisement, and 90% had neither the time nor the skills to manage it seriously.

  • Customer reviews — nobody was replying ("I still have a negative review from 2021 with no response").
  • Websites — either non-existent or a WordPress patched together in 2016 that took 8 seconds to load.
  • Bookings — happening by SMS or phone, lost in the shuffle.
  • Social media? "I don't have the time."

On the tooling side, each problem had its own SaaS: Trustpilot or Partoo for reviews, Wix or Shopify for the site, Zenchef or Deliverect for bookings, Hootsuite for social. The bill: €150 to €400 per month, 6 logins, 6 invoices, and a shopkeeper who churns in 3 months.

Voxtya was born from that observation: put everything in one place, let the AI do 80% of the work, let the owner keep control in two clicks.

A year later, 1,580 local businesses trust us, 24,800 Google reviews have been collected through Voxtya, and our customers save an average of 9 hours per month while seeing +45% visits on their Google listing. Here's what we learned.

Lesson 1: the Google Business Profile is the #1 channel, but badly exploited

Before Voxtya, 68% of our customers had fewer than 15 Google reviews. After 6 months with us, that drops to 11%. The median goes from 12 to 47 reviews.

Why? Because asking for a review at the right time, from the right customer, through the right channel is a scriptwriter's job, not a restaurateur's. We built three mechanics that actually work in the real world:

  1. "Wheel of fortune" QR code stuck in the window or at the counter. The customer scans, spins the wheel (a small reward to win — a free coffee, dessert, discount), and to spin they're asked for a Google review. In restaurants with a terrace, scan rate exceeds 20%.
  2. SMS/email follow-up post-visit (for artisans and wellness especially): 24 hours after the service, a direct link to the Google listing.
  3. Room QR codes for hoteliers.

Aggregated result: ×3.9 review volume vs. pre-Voxtya, at constant advertising budget.

Lesson 2: replying to 100% of reviews within 48h changes everything

Google has said it repeatedly: businesses that reply to their reviews are favored in the local pack. We measured it on our customer base.

Across 170 businesses tracked over 6 months:

  • Those replying to <30% of reviews: flat local visibility.
  • Those replying to 100% of reviews within 48 hours (via our AI drafting the reply, validated or not by the owner): +28% impressions on the listing on average.

The detail that matters: the tone of the reply. Copy-paste replies ("thanks for your review") do nothing. Replies that pick up a word from the customer ("thanks for your feedback on our new truffle menu") convert three times better into action — click to directions, click to site, call.

That's exactly what the AI does, in 3 seconds, 24/7. The human keeps control of sensitive cases (complaints, 1 or 2 stars).

Lesson 3: a fast site derived from the Google listing beats a "designer" site

Half of our customers had no website. The other half had one they considered "not great". We tested a radical hypothesis: auto-generate the site from the Google listing (address, hours, photos, menu, services), with clean design, fast (<1s LCP), and perfect technical SEO.

Result:

  • Go-live time: 3 minutes, not 3 weeks.
  • PageSpeed mobile score: 91/100 average, vs. 38/100 for our customers' existing sites.
  • Organic traffic at 3 months: ×2.3 on queries like "bakery + city".

The trap we avoided: don't sell a "site builder". We sell a site already built the day they sign up, that the customer can modify if they want. 88% of our customers change nothing — and that's fine.

Lesson 4: online bookings must be free (for the end customer)

Zenchef, TheFork, Resy charge €2 to €7 per booking, or a monthly fee that bites. For a 40-seat restaurant with a €25 average ticket, that's 10% of margin lost to commission.

At Voxtya the booking module is included in the Suite, commission-free. The 280 restaurants we equip have moved all their bookings direct from their Voxtya site and Google listing. Over 6 months, that represents ~€94,000 of commissions not paid to TheFork in total.

For artisans, the "booking module" becomes a "quote request form" with automatic follow-ups. Same mechanics, same free.

Lesson 5: AI is useful when it hands back control fast, not when it fakes it

We almost got this wrong by trying to automate everything. Voxtya's first version published posts on Google Business Profile and Instagram without validation, from detected events (new menu, new photo). Owners hated it. "That's not my voice."

The right mechanic: the AI proposes (post draft, reply draft, new photo draft), the owner validates in 2 clicks from their phone. The draft has to be perfect 80% of the time for validation to feel like a reflex. Below that, the owner stops opening the app.

Today, 9 out of 10 owners validate without edits. But the ability to edit is central — it's what separates "copilot" from "autopilot". Local business owners don't want autopilot on their voice.

What doesn't work (let's be honest)

  • We don't have a solution for businesses without walk-in customers (wholesalers, B2B). The "window QR review collection" model doesn't apply.
  • Chains with more than 20 locations deserve a more enterprise-oriented tool; we point them elsewhere.
  • Onboarding is still too manual for some trades: an auto garage needs specific categories our generic configurator doesn't cover well yet.

If you're building your own tool

  • Start from the Google listing. It's the source of truth, not your internal DB.
  • Don't ask for the Google Business API login before the customer has seen value. Google makes onboarding painful; absorb it, don't push it to the customer.
  • AI should propose, not publish. 2-click validation, always.
  • Make free what your competitors charge for (bookings, websites). You'll earn it back on the monthly plan, not on commission.

If these takeaways are useful, the tool that came out of it is Voxtya — 30-day free trial, from €29 per month, no commitment.

title: Security Risks of AI-Generated Code: Research and a Review Checklist
description:
Originally published on shipfastdev.com.

AI-generated code usually works, but it is often not secure. In Veracode's 2026 tests, models produced code that compiled almost 100% of the time, yet failed security checks on nearly 44% of tasks, a pass rate that has not improved since 2025. The fix is not to ban AI tools; it is to treat their output like code from a contractor you have never worked with: review it, scan it, and test it before it reaches production.

Below is a summary of the research, the failure patterns that come up again and again, and a review checklist you can hand to your developer or agency.

What the research found

Veracode: about half of security-relevant tasks fail, and it is not improving

In its 2025 GenAI Code Security Report, Veracode gave 80 curated coding tasks to more than 100 large language models. When a secure and an insecure approach were both possible, models chose the insecure one 45% of the time. Java was the riskiest language, with a security failure rate above 70%; Python, C# and JavaScript failed between 38% and 45% of the time. Models failed to defend against cross-site scripting in 86% of cases and log injection in 88%. Larger models did not perform significantly better than smaller ones.

The 2026 edition found the average security pass rate "sits at 56 percent — virtually unchanged since last year's report." The best model on its summer 2026 leaderboard reached 68%, which still means failing nearly one security task in three. Python code passed 63% of the time, Java only 30%. Coding-specialised models (51%) did no better than general-purpose ones (52%), and model size made no clear difference, although reasoning models kept an edge (56% against 51%).

Academic studies: vulnerable suggestions and overconfident users

  • An early study of GitHub Copilot, "Asleep at the Keyboard?" (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022), generated 1,689 programs across 89 security-relevant scenarios and found approximately 40% of them vulnerable.
  • A user study published at ACM CCS 2023 found that participants with an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code than those without, and were more likely to believe their code was secure.
  • A USENIX Security 2025 paper analysed 576,000 code samples from 16 models and found that at least 5.2% of packages suggested by commercial models and 21.7% by open-source models did not exist, with 205,474 unique invented package names. An attacker can publish a malicious package under a name that models tend to invent, and anyone who installs it without checking is compromised.

Team level: more changes, less stability

Google's 2025 DORA report found that AI adoption is linked to higher delivery throughput but still has a negative relationship with delivery stability. Its explanation applies directly to security: without strong automated testing and fast feedback loops, more change volume leads to more incidents.

Why AI-generated code fails security checks

Security usually depends on context the model does not have: which input comes from an untrusted user, who is allowed to see which record, which secrets exist in your environment. Cross-site scripting, which depends on knowing where a piece of data will be displayed, had one of the worst results in Veracode's 2025 tests (86% failure). The model writes code that does what you asked; whether it is safe depends on what you did not say.

The failure patterns to look for

  • Untrusted input reaching output or queries: cross-site scripting, SQL injection, log injection.
  • Missing authorisation checks: an endpoint that checks the user is logged in, but not that the record belongs to them.
  • Secrets in code: API keys pasted into source files or front-end bundles.
  • Invented or outdated dependencies: packages that do not exist, or old versions with known vulnerabilities.
  • Insecure defaults: permissive CORS, debug mode on, verbose error messages in production.
  • Weak cryptography or home-made auth instead of the framework's built-in tools.

A security review checklist for AI-generated code

You don't need to read code to use this list. Ask your developer to confirm each point for every feature that touches users, payments or data. Items 1 to 4 apply before any change is merged, 5 to 7 cover dependencies and secrets, and 8 to 12 cover testing and process.

  1. A human who understands the code has reviewed every AI-generated change, line by line.
  2. Every endpoint checks authorisation (who can access this record), not just authentication.
  3. All user input is validated on the server, and output is escaped by the framework (no raw HTML rendering of user content).
  4. Database access uses the framework's query builder or parameterised queries, never string-built SQL.
  5. Every new package was checked: it exists, is maintained, and is the one the developer meant to install.
  6. A dependency audit runs automatically (for example npm audit, composer audit or GitHub Dependabot).
  7. No secret is committed to the repository or shipped to the browser; secret scanning is enabled.
  8. Automated tests cover login, permissions and payment flows, and run on every change. End-to-end tests such as the Playwright setup we use catch broken access rules early.
  9. A static analysis (SAST) tool runs in CI on every pull request.
  10. Production runs with debug off, restrictive CORS and generic error pages.
  11. AI agents cannot touch production data or credentials directly.
  12. Someone owns security decisions, and you know who.

Questions to ask your developer or agency

  • Which AI tools do you use, and what is your review rule for their output?
  • What runs automatically on every pull request: tests, dependency audit, static analysis, secret scanning?
  • How are authorisation rules tested?
  • Who would notice if a new package did not exist yesterday?

These questions belong in any evaluation of a development partner. If your app was built mainly with an AI app builder, read where vibe-coded MVPs break as well: missing data-access rules are the most common problem there.

Frequently asked questions

Is AI-generated code secure?

Not by default. Veracode's 2026 tests found an average security pass rate of 56%, unchanged from 2025, even though almost all generated code compiled. It needs the same review and testing as any other code, and arguably more.

Which programming language is riskiest for AI-generated code?

In Veracode's tests, Java: a 30% security pass rate in 2026, against 63% for Python. Language matters less than review, though: every language failed a significant share of tasks.

Can an AI tool review its own code for security?

It can help spot issues, but the same models chose insecure options in a large share of Veracode's tasks. Use AI review as one layer, alongside static analysis, dependency audits, tests and a human reviewer.

Do I need a security audit for my MVP?

If it handles personal data, payments or logins, at least run through the checklist above before launch. A full external audit makes sense once you have real users or sensitive data at scale.

Sources

  1. LLMs Are Getting Smarter but Not Safer: Veracode 2026 GenAI Code Security Report, Veracode, 2026-07
  2. AI-Generated Code Poses Major Security Risks in Nearly Half of All Development Tasks, Veracode Research Reveals, Veracode, 2025-07
  3. Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions (IEEE S&P 2022), Pearce, Ahmad, Tan, Dolan-Gavitt, Karri (arXiv), 2021-12
  4. Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (ACM CCS 2023), Perry, Srivastava, Kumar, Boneh (arXiv), 2023-12
  5. We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs (USENIX Security 2025), Spracklen et al. (arXiv), 2025-03
  6. Announcing the 2025 DORA Report, Google Cloud, 2025-09

title: A Backdoor Sat in the Firmware Partition of 1.3 Million Set-Top Boxes
description:
TL;DR

  • A botnet is a network of compromised devices that a remote operator controls, usually to rent out the devices or to run fraud at someone else's expense.
  • On 2 November 2026 Google Threat Intelligence Group disclosed that Google and its partners dismantled XCPE, a backdoor that enrolled more than 1.3 million Android set-top boxes, and attributed it with high confidence to Videostrong Technology, an Android OEM and ODM.
  • The backdoor sat in the firmware partition at android.uid.system privilege, reinstalled itself from the /oem/ partition when a user removed it, and handed module execution to a loader called com.abc.nexus.
  • Command and control runs in two stages: an HTTP POST that returns configuration, then a persistent MQTT connection to a broker that delivers app installs, shell commands, screen captures and network reconnaissance.
